targetText: The splitting of a single whole and the cognition of its contradictory parts (see the quotation from Philo on Heraclitus at the beginning of Section III, “On Cognition,” in Lasalle’s book on Heraclitus[1]) is the essence (one of the “essentials,” one of the principal, if not the principal, characteristics or features) of dialectics.
explanation: Lenin traces dialectics from ancient Greek philosophy (Heraclitus) through Hegel to Marx, identifying its primary principle: analyzing any phenomenon requires discovering its internally divided, contradictory aspects.

targetText: The two basic (or two possible? Or two historically observable?) conceptions of development (evolution) are: development as decrease and increase, as repetition, and development as a unity of opposites (the division of a unity into mutually exclusive opposites and their reciprocal relation).
explanation: Lenin contrasts vulgar evolutionism with revolutionary dialectics. The former views change merely as gradual quantitative growth without breaks or leaps; the latter identifies the source of motion within the internal struggle of opposites.
context: Following the collapse of the Second International in 1914, Lenin retreated to the Bern library to study Hegel. He realized that reformists like Plekhanov and Kautsky had abandoned dialectics for vulgar, mechanical evolutionism, which led them to preach class collaboration and support the imperialist war.

targetText: The first conception is lifeless, pale and dry. The second is living. The second alone furnishes the key to the “self-movement” of everything existing; it alone furnishes the key to “leaps,” to the “break in continuity,” to the “transformation into the opposite,” to the destruction of the old and the emergence of the new.
explanation: Dialectics alone explains qualitative transformations and revolutionary ruptures in history. Without the unity of opposites, motion must be attributed to an external cause or metaphysical prime mover.

targetText: The unity (coincidence, identity, equal action) of opposites is conditional, temporary, transitory, relative. The struggle of mutually exclusive opposites is absolute, just as development and motion are absolute.
explanation: A fundamental law of dialectical materialism: equilibrium and stability are always temporary and relative, while contradiction, struggle, and historical transformation are eternal and absolute.

targetText: Human knowledge is not (or does not follow) a straight line, but a curve, which endlessly approximates a series of circles, a spiral.
explanation: Human cognition does not progress in a simple, flat linear line; it develops dialectically in a spiral, revisiting earlier stages at a higher, richer level of conceptual comprehension.

targetText: Rectilinearity and one-sidedness, woodenness and petrification, subjectivism and subjective blindness: voilà the epistemological roots of idealism. And clerical obscrutantism (= philosophical idealism), of course, has epistemological roots, it is not groundless; it is a sterile flower undoubtedly, but a sterile flower that grows on the living tree of living, fertile, genuine, powerful, omnipotent, objective, absolute human knowledge.
explanation: Lenin provides a dialectical materialist explanation for why philosophical idealism and religious mystification persist: they arise when human thought isolates one aspect of knowledge into an exaggerated, one-sided absolute, anchored by reactionary class interests.
